analysis.one_liner: Tightens tailpipe pollution limits for cars and light trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill to tighten car emission standards died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten Clean Air Act rules to cap tailpipe emissions of organic gases, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and particulate matter from cars and small trucks starting with model years after 2003. It also required vehicles to stay within those limits for 10 years or 100,000 miles. It was referred to committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe vehicle pollution — city dwellers, commuters, and communities near highways — would gain cleaner air, since the bill caps smog-forming gases, carbon monoxide, and soot from new cars and light trucks. Requiring engines to meet the limits for 10 years or 100,000 miles means vehicles stay clean for their whole life on the road, not just when new.

how_it_helps.text: Sets hard per-mile limits on four pollutants — organic gases (NMOG), nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and particulate matter — for light-duty vehicles and trucks weighing 3,750 lbs or less, starting with model years after January 1, 2003.

Extends the required useful life to 10 years or 100,000 miles, so cars and trucks must keep meeting the emission limits for as long as most people own them, rather than being allowed to pollute more as they age.
The CRS summary confirms the bill revised Clean Air Act standards for organic gases, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and particulate matter from light-duty vehicles and trucks.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the engineering cost of building cleaner engines for model years after 2003, and new-car buyers would likely see some of that cost passed along in vehicle prices. Oil companies could also face pressure as cleaner-burning vehicles reduce demand for the highest-emission fuels.

drawbacks.text: Tighter per-mile emission limits cost automakers real money in engine and catalyst engineering, and some of that cost would reach new-car buyers through higher prices.
The bill fixes a single rigid table of limits with no compliance flexibility or phase-in options, which a good-faith critic could argue is a costlier way to cut pollution than a more flexible design.
Because the standards would not begin until model years after 2003, most drivers would see no benefit for over a decade after passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cleaner air is a broad benefit that reaches everyone who breathes, while the cost falls on a small set of manufacturers and is spread thinly across new-car prices. The bill's weak points are its long lead time — nothing improves until 2003 — and a rigid one-size table with no flexibility. On balance the gains outweigh the costs, but the bill was written to matter only in the distant future, which made it easy to ignore.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 1993 — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Wayne Owens of Utah introduced the bill on March 25, 1992 to strengthen automobile emission standards under the Clean Air Act.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which held no action on it.
On June 15, 1992 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it remained until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never reached a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill died: they avoided binding per-mile emission limits and a 10-year/100,000-mile useful-life requirement for future model years, while the public got no cleaner air.

for.name: Wayne Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten car and light-truck emission standards; it was his bill alone.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never brought it up for committee action.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 15, 1992 and held it without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill's only sponsor was a lone Democrat with zero cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan split to measure.

industries.note: The bill would have forced stricter per-mile limits on smog gases, carbon monoxide, and soot for cars and light trucks built after 2003, plus a 10-year/100,000-mile durability requirement. That means significant engine and emissions-control engineering spending, some of which reaches buyers as higher prices — but it never happened, so the industry's standards stayed where the 1990 Clean Air Act left them.
